name: Common Cold
summary: A mild viral infection of the nose and throat. It usually clears up on its own within 7–10 days.
self_care: Rest and drink plenty of fluids (water, warm soups, herbal tea).
Gargle with warm salt water to soothe a sore throat.
Use steam inhalation or a saline nasal spray to ease congestion.
Honey in warm water can soothe a cough (not for children under 1 year).
medicines: Paracetamol for aches or fever — follow the dose on the label.
Saline nasal drops or spray for a blocked nose.
Antibiotics do NOT help a cold, because it is caused by a virus.
see_doctor: Symptoms last more than 10 days or get worse after improving.
Fever above 39°C (102°F) or lasting more than 3 days.
Difficulty breathing, wheezing or chest pain.
Severe sinus pain or ear pain.
prevention: Wash hands often with soap for at least 20 seconds.
Avoid touching your eyes, nose and mouth.
Keep away from people who are sick and cover your coughs and sneezes.
Eat a balanced diet with fruits and vegetables and sleep well.

name: Influenza (Flu)
summary: A contagious viral infection that comes on suddenly with fever, body aches and exhaustion. Usually more severe than a cold.
self_care: Rest at home and avoid contact with others until 24 hours after the fever is gone.
Drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.
Keep warm and get as much sleep as you can.
medicines: Paracetamol or ibuprofen can lower fever and ease aches — follow the label.
A doctor may prescribe antiviral medicine if started early or if you are at high risk.
see_doctor: You are over 65, pregnant, or have a long-term condition such as diabetes, asthma or heart disease.
Shortness of breath, chest pain or confusion.
Symptoms do not improve after 7 days.
Signs of dehydration (very little urine, dizziness).
prevention: Get the annual flu vaccine.
Wash hands regularly and use hand sanitiser.
Stay home when sick and wear a mask in crowded places during flu season.

name: COVID-19
summary: A respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Severity ranges from mild cold-like symptoms to serious illness.
self_care: Take a COVID-19 test if available and isolate while you have symptoms.
Rest, stay hydrated and monitor your temperature.
If you have a pulse oximeter, check your oxygen level regularly.
medicines: Paracetamol for fever and aches — follow the label.
High-risk people may be eligible for antiviral treatment; ask a doctor early.
see_doctor: Oxygen saturation below 94% or difficulty breathing.
Persistent chest pain or pressure.
Confusion, bluish lips or inability to stay awake — seek emergency care.
prevention: Stay up to date with recommended vaccinations.
Wear a well-fitted mask in crowded indoor spaces.
Improve ventilation and wash hands frequently.

name: Viral Fever
summary: A raised body temperature caused by a viral infection. Most viral fevers settle within 3–5 days with rest.
self_care: Rest and drink plenty of fluids — water, ORS, coconut water, soups.
Wear light clothing and sponge with lukewarm (not cold) water.
Eat light, easily digestible food.
medicines: Paracetamol to bring down fever — follow the label and do not exceed the maximum daily dose.
Avoid giving aspirin to children and teenagers.
see_doctor: Fever lasts more than 3 days or is above 39.4°C (103°F).
Rash, severe headache, stiff neck or sensitivity to light.
Bleeding from gums or nose, or severe abdominal pain (possible dengue).
Confusion, seizures or difficulty breathing.
prevention: Wash hands regularly and maintain good hygiene.
Drink clean, safe water.
Avoid close contact with people who are ill.

name: Dengue Fever
summary: A mosquito-borne viral infection common in tropical regions, causing high fever and severe body and joint pain.
self_care: Rest and drink lots of fluids — ORS, water, coconut water, juices.
Monitor how much you drink and urinate.
medicines: Paracetamol for fever and pain — follow the label.
Do NOT take ibuprofen, aspirin or other NSAIDs, as they can increase bleeding risk.
see_doctor: See a doctor for a blood test (platelet count) if you suspect dengue.
Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, or blood in vomit/stool — go to hospital immediately.
Restlessness, extreme tiredness or cold clammy skin.
prevention: Use mosquito repellent and wear long sleeves.
Remove standing water around your home (coolers, pots, tyres).
Use mosquito nets and window screens.

name: Malaria
summary: A serious mosquito-borne parasitic infection causing cycles of fever, chills and sweating. It needs prompt testing and treatment.
self_care: Get a blood test as soon as possible — malaria needs prescription treatment.
Rest and stay well hydrated.
medicines: Malaria is treated with prescription antimalarial medicines chosen by a doctor based on the test result.
Paracetamol can help with fever while you arrange a test.
see_doctor: Any fever with chills after being in a malaria area — get tested the same day.
Confusion, drowsiness, seizures, yellow eyes or dark urine — emergency.
prevention: Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets.
Use repellent and cover arms and legs at dusk and dawn.
Ask a doctor about preventive medicine before travelling to high-risk areas.

name: Typhoid Fever
summary: A bacterial infection spread through contaminated food and water, with a fever that rises gradually over several days.
self_care: See a doctor for diagnosis — typhoid needs antibiotics.
Drink plenty of safe fluids and eat soft, light meals.
medicines: Typhoid is treated with prescription antibiotics; complete the full course.
Paracetamol can help with fever.
see_doctor: Fever lasting more than 3 days, especially after eating outside or drinking unsafe water.
Severe abdominal pain, blood in stool or confusion — emergency.
prevention: Drink boiled or bottled water.
Eat freshly cooked hot food and avoid raw street food.
Wash hands before eating and after using the toilet.
Typhoid vaccines are available — ask your doctor.

name: Gastroenteritis (Stomach Flu / Food Poisoning)
summary: Inflammation of the stomach and intestines, usually from a virus or contaminated food. Most people recover in 1–3 days.
self_care: Sip ORS (oral rehydration solution) frequently to replace lost fluids and salts.
Eat bland foods once you can — rice, bananas, toast, curd.
Avoid dairy, fried, spicy food, caffeine and alcohol until you recover.
medicines: ORS is the most important treatment.
Zinc supplements are recommended for children with diarrhoea — ask a pharmacist.
Avoid anti-diarrhoea medicine if you have blood in stool or high fever.
see_doctor: Cannot keep fluids down for more than 24 hours.
Blood in vomit or stool, or severe abdominal pain.
Signs of dehydration: very little urine, dizziness, dry mouth.
Diarrhoea lasting more than 3 days (or 24 hours in infants).
prevention: Wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating.
Drink safe water and eat food that is freshly cooked.
Store food properly and wash fruits and vegetables.

name: Acid Reflux (GERD)
summary: Stomach acid flowing back into the food pipe, causing a burning feeling in the chest, especially after meals or when lying down.
self_care: Eat smaller meals and avoid lying down for 3 hours after eating.
Raise the head of your bed by 15–20 cm.
Cut down on spicy, fried and fatty food, coffee, chocolate and alcohol.
Stop smoking and keep a healthy weight.
medicines: Antacids from a pharmacy can relieve occasional heartburn — follow the label.
If you need antacids often, a doctor can advise on longer-term options.
see_doctor: Heartburn more than twice a week or not helped by antacids.
Difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood or black stools.
Unexplained weight loss.
Chest pain with sweating or breathlessness may be a heart problem — seek emergency care.
prevention: Maintain a healthy weight.
Avoid trigger foods and late-night meals.
Avoid tight clothing around the waist.

name: Migraine
summary: A moderate to severe throbbing headache, often on one side, sometimes with nausea and sensitivity to light or sound.
self_care: Rest in a quiet, dark room.
Apply a cold pack to the forehead or back of the neck.
Keep a headache diary to spot triggers (sleep, stress, certain foods, skipped meals).
medicines: Paracetamol or ibuprofen taken early in an attack can help — follow the label.
Frequent migraines can be treated with prescription medicines; see a doctor.
see_doctor: Headaches are getting more frequent or severe.
Pain-relief medicines are needed more than 2–3 days a week.
Sudden, severe 'worst ever' headache, or headache with weakness, confusion, slurred speech or stiff neck — emergency.
prevention: Keep a regular sleep and meal schedule.
Stay hydrated and limit caffeine and alcohol.
Manage stress with exercise, yoga or relaxation techniques.

name: Tension Headache
summary: The most common type of headache — a dull, tight pressure like a band around the head, often linked to stress, posture or screen time.
self_care: Take regular breaks from screens and check your posture.
Gently massage your neck and shoulders, or apply warmth.
Drink enough water and get regular sleep.
Try relaxation, stretching or a short walk.
medicines: Paracetamol or ibuprofen can relieve occasional headaches — follow the label.
Avoid taking painkillers more than 2–3 days a week, as this can cause rebound headaches.
see_doctor: Headaches happen most days or interfere with daily life.
Headache after a head injury.
Headache with fever, stiff neck, rash, confusion or vision loss — seek urgent care.
prevention: Manage stress and take screen breaks (20-20-20 rule).
Exercise regularly.
Keep good posture at your desk.

name: Sinusitis
summary: Swelling of the sinuses, usually after a cold, causing facial pain, a blocked nose and thick nasal discharge.
self_care: Steam inhalation and saline nasal rinses can clear mucus.
Apply a warm compress over the face.
Rest and stay hydrated.
medicines: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain — follow the label.
Decongestant sprays should not be used for more than a few days.
see_doctor: Symptoms last more than 10 days or keep coming back.
Severe pain, swelling around the eyes, or vision changes — seek urgent care.
High fever or confusion.
prevention: Treat colds and allergies early.
Avoid smoke and other irritants.
Use a humidifier in dry weather.

name: Allergic Rhinitis (Hay Fever)
summary: An allergic reaction to things like dust, pollen or pet dander, causing sneezing, an itchy runny nose and watery eyes — without fever.
self_care: Identify and avoid triggers such as dust, pollen, mould or pets.
Rinse your nose with saline solution.
Keep windows closed on high-pollen days and wash bedding weekly in hot water.
medicines: Non-drowsy antihistamines from a pharmacy can relieve symptoms — follow the label.
A doctor may recommend a steroid nasal spray for frequent symptoms.
see_doctor: Symptoms affect sleep, work or study.
Wheezing or shortness of breath.
Over-the-counter remedies are not helping.
prevention: Use dust-mite-proof pillow and mattress covers.
Vacuum and dust regularly (with a mask if sensitive).
Shower and change clothes after being outdoors on high-pollen days.

name: Pharyngitis / Strep Throat
summary: Infection of the throat or tonsils. A bacterial (strep) infection usually comes with fever and swollen glands and no cough.
self_care: Gargle with warm salt water several times a day.
Drink warm liquids and eat soft foods.
Rest your voice.
medicines: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever — follow the label.
Strep throat needs antibiotics prescribed by a doctor; viral sore throats do not.
see_doctor: Sore throat with fever and swollen glands but no cough.
Symptoms last more than a week.
Difficulty breathing, drooling, or unable to swallow fluids — seek urgent care.
prevention: Wash hands often.
Don't share cups, utensils or toothbrushes.
Replace your toothbrush after an infection.

name: Acute Bronchitis
summary: Inflammation of the airways in the lungs, usually after a cold, causing a cough with mucus that can last up to 3 weeks.
self_care: Rest and drink plenty of fluids to loosen mucus.
Use steam inhalation or a humidifier.
Avoid smoking and smoky environments.
medicines: Paracetamol for fever or chest discomfort — follow the label.
Honey in warm water can soothe a cough (not for children under 1).
Antibiotics are usually not needed for viral bronchitis.
see_doctor: Cough lasts more than 3 weeks.
High fever, coughing up blood, or chest pain.
Shortness of breath that is getting worse.
prevention: Don't smoke and avoid second-hand smoke.
Get vaccinated against flu.
Wash hands frequently.

name: Asthma
summary: A long-term condition where the airways narrow and swell, causing wheezing, breathlessness and chest tightness, often triggered by allergens, exercise or cold air.
self_care: Follow your personal asthma action plan if you have one.
Identify and avoid triggers (dust, smoke, pollen, cold air, pets).
Sit upright and breathe slowly during symptoms.
medicines: Asthma is managed with inhalers prescribed by a doctor (reliever and preventer).
Carry your reliever inhaler with you at all times if you have one.
see_doctor: See a doctor for diagnosis if you have recurring wheezing or breathlessness.
Reliever inhaler isn't helping, lips turn blue, or you can't speak in full sentences — call emergency services (112) immediately.
prevention: Take preventer medicines as prescribed, even when well.
Keep your home free of dust and smoke.
Get the annual flu vaccine.

name: Type 2 Diabetes
summary: A long-term condition where blood sugar is too high because the body doesn't make or use insulin properly. Early diagnosis prevents complications.
self_care: Get a blood sugar test (fasting glucose or HbA1c) to confirm.
Choose whole grains, vegetables and lean protein; cut down on sugar and refined carbs.
Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
medicines: Diabetes treatment (tablets or insulin) must be prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Never start, stop or change diabetes medicine without medical advice.
see_doctor: You have several of these symptoms — get tested soon.
Very high or very low sugar readings, vomiting, confusion or fruity-smelling breath — emergency.
prevention: Keep a healthy weight and stay physically active.
Limit sugary drinks, sweets and processed foods.
Get regular check-ups if diabetes runs in your family.

name: High Blood Pressure (Hypertension)
summary: Blood pressure consistently at or above 130/80 mmHg. It often has no symptoms, which is why it is called the 'silent killer'.
self_care: Check your blood pressure regularly and keep a record.
Reduce salt to less than 5 g (1 teaspoon) a day.
Exercise regularly, keep a healthy weight, and limit alcohol.
Stop smoking and manage stress.
medicines: Blood pressure medicines must be prescribed by a doctor and taken every day as directed.
see_doctor: Readings repeatedly above 130/80 mmHg.
Reading above 180/120 with chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, vision changes or severe headache — emergency.
prevention: Eat a diet rich in fruits, vegetables and whole grains (DASH diet).
Limit salt, processed food and alcohol.
Stay active and maintain a healthy weight.

name: Coronary Heart Disease / Angina
summary: Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart, which can cause chest pain (angina) and lead to heart attacks. Try the Heart Risk check in this app.
self_care: If you have chest pain right now, stop all activity and call emergency services (112).
Long-term: eat a heart-healthy diet, exercise, stop smoking and control BP, sugar and cholesterol.
medicines: Heart medicines must be prescribed by a cardiologist.
During a suspected heart attack, emergency services may advise chewing aspirin if you are not allergic — follow their instructions.
see_doctor: Chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes, especially with sweating, breathlessness or pain spreading to the arm or jaw — call 112 now.
Chest discomfort on exertion that goes away with rest — see a cardiologist soon.
prevention: Don't smoke.
Exercise at least 30 minutes on most days.
Eat more fruits, vegetables and whole grains; limit saturated fats and salt.
Check blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol regularly.

name: Iron-Deficiency Anaemia
summary: A low level of healthy red blood cells, often due to lack of iron, which makes you feel tired and short of breath.
self_care: Get a blood test (haemoglobin and iron levels) to confirm.
Eat iron-rich foods: green leafy vegetables, lentils, beans, jaggery, eggs, meat.
Have vitamin C (citrus fruit) with meals to improve iron absorption; avoid tea or coffee with meals.
medicines: Iron supplements should be taken only after a doctor confirms anaemia — follow their dosage.
see_doctor: Persistent tiredness, breathlessness or paleness.
Heavy menstrual periods or blood in stool.
Chest pain or fainting — seek urgent care.
prevention: Eat a balanced, iron-rich diet.
Treat heavy periods or worm infections.
Pregnant women should follow their doctor's advice on supplements.

name: Hypothyroidism (Underactive Thyroid)
summary: The thyroid gland does not produce enough hormone, slowing the body's metabolism. It is easily diagnosed with a blood test.
self_care: Ask your doctor for a thyroid function test (TSH).
Eat a balanced diet and use iodised salt.
medicines: Thyroid hormone replacement is prescribed by a doctor and dosed using regular blood tests.
see_doctor: Several of these symptoms for weeks — get a TSH test.
Pregnant or planning pregnancy with thyroid symptoms.
prevention: Use iodised salt.
Get regular thyroid check-ups if it runs in your family.

name: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
summary: A bacterial infection of the bladder or urinary tract causing burning while urinating and a frequent urge to go.
self_care: Drink plenty of water to help flush out bacteria.
Don't hold in urine — go when you need to.
A warm pad on the lower abdomen can ease discomfort.
medicines: UTIs usually need antibiotics prescribed by a doctor — complete the full course.
Paracetamol can relieve pain.
see_doctor: See a doctor if you have UTI symptoms — especially if pregnant, male, or symptoms recur.
Fever, back or side pain, or vomiting may mean a kidney infection — seek care the same day.
prevention: Drink enough water daily.
Wipe from front to back after using the toilet.
Urinate after sexual intercourse.
Avoid scented products in the genital area.

name: Depression
summary: A common, treatable mental health condition with persistent low mood or loss of interest lasting two weeks or more. You are not alone, and help works.
self_care: Talk to someone you trust about how you feel.
Keep a simple routine: regular sleep, meals, and some daily movement or sunlight.
Set small, achievable goals and be kind to yourself.
Limit alcohol and avoid recreational drugs.
medicines: Talking therapies (like CBT) and/or prescribed medicines are effective — a doctor or psychiatrist can advise what suits you.
Never start or stop antidepressants without medical guidance.
see_doctor: Low mood lasting more than 2 weeks or affecting daily life.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out now: Tele-MANAS 14416 (India, 24×7, free) or emergency 112.
prevention: Stay connected with friends and family.
Exercise regularly and get enough sleep.
Seek help early when stress builds up.

name: Anxiety Disorder
summary: Ongoing, excessive worry that is hard to control, often with physical symptoms like a racing heart, restlessness and poor sleep.
self_care: Try slow breathing: breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4, out for 6.
Exercise regularly and reduce caffeine.
Write down worries and break problems into small steps.
Try mindfulness, yoga or meditation apps.
medicines: Talking therapy (CBT) is very effective; a doctor may also suggest medicine.
Avoid self-medicating with alcohol or sleeping pills.
see_doctor: Anxiety interferes with work, study or relationships.
Frequent panic attacks.
Chest pain with breathlessness should be checked urgently to rule out heart problems.
prevention: Keep a regular sleep schedule.
Limit caffeine, alcohol and screen time before bed.
Talk about your feelings early.

name: Insomnia
summary: Regular difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, leaving you tired during the day.
self_care: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.
Avoid screens for an hour before bed and keep the bedroom dark and cool.
Avoid caffeine after 2 pm, heavy meals and alcohol at night.
If you can't sleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something relaxing.
medicines: Sleeping pills should only be used short-term under medical advice.
CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is the most effective long-term treatment.
see_doctor: Poor sleep for more than 3 weeks affecting daily life.
Loud snoring with gasping or pauses in breathing (possible sleep apnoea).
prevention: Keep a consistent sleep routine.
Get daylight and exercise during the day.
Manage stress.

name: Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye)
summary: Inflammation of the thin layer covering the eye, causing redness, itching and discharge. Often viral and contagious.
self_care: Clean eyelids gently with cooled boiled water and a clean cotton pad.
Don't rub your eyes; wash hands often.
Don't share towels or pillows; avoid contact lenses until better.
medicines: Lubricating eye drops can soothe irritation.
Antibiotic or anti-allergy drops should be used only if a doctor or pharmacist advises.
see_doctor: Eye pain, sensitivity to light or blurred vision.
Symptoms in a newborn baby.
No improvement after 1 week.
prevention: Wash hands frequently and avoid touching your eyes.
Don't share eye makeup, towels or eye drops.

name: Acne
summary: A common skin condition where hair follicles get blocked with oil and dead skin, causing pimples, blackheads and whiteheads.
self_care: Wash your face twice a day with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water — no more.
Don't squeeze or pick spots; this can cause scarring.
Use oil-free, 'non-comedogenic' moisturiser and makeup; remove makeup before bed.
Wash your hair regularly and keep it off your face.
medicines: Pharmacy creams with benzoyl peroxide or adapalene can help mild acne — follow the label.
Moderate or severe acne may need prescription treatment from a dermatologist.
see_doctor: Acne is painful, leaving scars, or not improving after 2–3 months.
Acne is affecting your confidence or mood.
prevention: Keep a gentle skincare routine.
Change pillowcases regularly.
Shower after sweating.

name: Chickenpox
summary: A highly contagious viral infection that causes an itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters, mostly in children.
self_care: Stay home until all blisters have crusted over (usually 5 days after the rash appears).
Trim nails and avoid scratching; calamine lotion and cool baths can soothe itching.
Drink plenty of fluids.
medicines: Paracetamol for fever — do NOT use ibuprofen or aspirin with chickenpox.
A doctor may prescribe antivirals for adults, pregnant women or people with weak immunity.
see_doctor: You are pregnant, an adult, or have a weakened immune system.
Blisters become red, hot or painful (infection).
Difficulty breathing, severe headache, confusion or stiff neck — emergency.
prevention: The chickenpox (varicella) vaccine is safe and effective.
Avoid contact with infected people until their blisters crust over.

name: Lower Back Pain
summary: Very common pain in the lower back, usually from muscle strain or posture. Most cases get better within a few weeks.
self_care: Keep moving gently — bed rest slows recovery.
Use heat or cold packs for 15–20 minutes at a time.
Do gentle stretches and check your sitting posture.
Lift with your knees, not your back.
medicines: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for short-term pain relief — follow the label.
see_doctor: Pain lasts more than 6 weeks or keeps getting worse.
Numbness around the groin/buttocks, loss of bladder or bowel control, or weakness in the legs — emergency.
Back pain with fever, weight loss or after a fall/injury.
prevention: Exercise regularly to strengthen core and back muscles.
Keep a healthy weight.
Take breaks from long periods of sitting.

name: Dehydration / Heat Exhaustion
summary: The body loses more fluid than it takes in, often in hot weather or after vomiting/diarrhoea, causing thirst, dizziness and dark urine.
self_care: Move to a cool, shaded place and lie down with legs raised.
Sip water or ORS slowly and steadily.
Cool the skin with a damp cloth or fan.
medicines: ORS (oral rehydration solution) is the best treatment.
see_doctor: No improvement after 30 minutes of rest and fluids.
Confusion, very high body temperature, hot dry skin, seizures or fainting — this may be heatstroke: call 112.
prevention: Drink water regularly, especially in hot weather and during exercise.
Avoid the midday sun and wear light, loose clothing.
Limit alcohol and caffeine in hot weather.
